d is the ratio of a provider’s model-development energy to its request-serving energy over a reporting period. For a provider v, development accelerator energy is E\_dev(v) \= d(v) × E\_acc(v), where E\_acc(v) is the §6 serving accelerator energy summed across that provider’s models.

| Source | Basis | d | Grade |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Epoch AI | Anthropic 2025: $4.1bn dev vs $2.7bn serving | 1.52 | B |
| SemiAnalysis | Lab compute: \~50% research, 10% training, 40% serving | 1.50 | C |
| Adopted | The two estimates agree to within 2% | 1.5 | — |

The Epoch AI figure (2026) is reconstructed from Anthropic’s reported revenue, gross margin and research and development expense for 2025\. The SemiAnalysis figure (2026) is derived from how a laboratory divides its accelerators. Two methods that share no inputs return the same value; that convergence, rather than the precision of either figure alone, is what supports the adopted value.

A single value is applied to every provider. Values calculated per provider differ by about 16%, against a relative uncertainty on each of about 53%; the difference between providers is a third of the uncertainty within either, so the two cannot be distinguished, and presenting them separately would assert a precision the evidence does not support. The factor register retains one row per provider, so that a provider publishing a specific figure can be moved to it without disturbing the rest.

The direction of travel is upward, not downward. SemiAnalysis reports that laboratories are already allocating a rising share of accelerator capacity to development, on the reasoning that the return on internal use exceeds the return on serving the same capacity externally. The value is reviewed quarterly for this reason (§13.4).

## 11.4 Provider classification

Revision A8 of the Scope 3 Standard revision restricts corporate-level allocation to homogeneous value-chain partners. Anthropic and OpenAI are homogeneous within the meaning of Box 7.4: their operations consist substantially of developing and serving language models, with emissions intensity uniform across the business. Diversified providers fall outside that permission, and a more granular level is required for them.

Google published a 60 / 40 split of inference to training for its machine-learning fleet for the three years to 2022\. That figure is first-party and energy-denominated, a stronger measurement basis than any other observation relied on here. It is nonetheless not applied. It covers Google’s entire machine-learning estate, most of which is search ranking, advertising and recommendation serving — large inference workloads carrying little frontier development behind them — and is therefore not representative of a frontier model line. Section 7.3 of the Scope 3 Standard scores technological and temporal representativeness alongside reliability, and the figure fails on both. It is recorded as the lower bound of the range.

No provider is excluded for want of a specific figure. A provider without one takes the adopted value and the data level is recorded accordingly. A provider that publishes nothing must not receive a lower figure than one that does.

## 11.5 Application in the chain

d applies to serving accelerator energy, before the uplift chain of §7. Development energy then carries the host uplift and PUE but not the idle uplift. The idle term covers serving capacity held ready to meet latency requirements (§7.3); development work is scheduled and holds no equivalent reserve. The two chains are × 1.50 × 1.10 × 1.45 \= × 2.39 for serving, and × 1.50 × 1.45 \= × 2.18 for development, GPU-served.

Development energy is converted to carbon at the serving region’s grid intensity, because no provider discloses where model development is performed. This is a declared simplification, carried as a §13.2 scenario row rather than left implicit. Embodied IT hardware and data-center construction apply to development energy on the same basis as serving energy.

## 11.6 Open-weight models

Where a provider serves a model it did not build, d for that provider applies, and will be small: an inference host performs little development of its own. The energy the model’s builder expended in training it is not allocated. The customer has no transactional relationship with that party and consumes none of its output, so no allocation basis exists, and folding it into d would allocate one company’s emissions using another company’s output share. It is quantified from published training compute and reported as an excluded amount with the reason stated, meeting the requirement in Revisions B1 and B2 to quantify a source before excluding it.

## 11.7 Measurement basis and direction of error

The values adopted are ratios of compute spending, not of energy. Development and serving are procured on different terms and run at different sustained utilization, and both differences run the same way: a dollar of development compute buys more accelerator-hours, and draws more power per hour, than a dollar of serving compute. d therefore understates the energy ratio. No correction is applied, because no source relied upon quantifies the gap. Obtaining a defensible conversion, or a provider disclosure stated in energy terms, is the single change that would most improve this factor.

One assumption runs the other way. Embodied intensity is derived at an assumed 40% average tray power (§12); development hardware runs materially harder, so the intensity properly applicable to development energy is lower than the value applied, and that term is overstated. The two errors are opposed. Both are disclosed rather than one being corrected and the other left in place.

# 12. The assembled calculation

Everything except the period’s token counts is fixed at methodology level and versioned in the factor register.

**Step 1 — serving accelerator energy. For each model m:**

E\_acc(m) \= Tᵢₙ(m)·ēᵢₙ(m) \+ T\_c(m)·r(m)·ēᵢₙ(m) \+ Tₒᵤₜ(m)·ēₒᵤₜ(m) E\_acc \= Σₘ E\_acc(m)

Step 2 — development accelerator energy. For each provider v: E\_dev(v) \= d(v) × E\_acc(v), with d \= 1.5 (§11.3). E\_dev \= Σᵥ E\_dev(v)

**Step 3 — facility energy.**

E\_fac \= E\_acc × 1.50 × 1.10 × 1.45 \+ E\_dev × 1.50 × 1.45 (GPU-served) E\_fac \= E\_acc × 1.43 × 1.10 × 1.45 \+ E\_dev × 1.43 × 1.45 (TPU-served)

Idle and PUE are universal cross-provider defaults; only the host term is hardware-class-specific. The idle uplift applies to serving energy alone, for the reason given in §11.5.

**Step 4 — operational emissions. Operational (LB) \= E\_fac × CI, with the rung recorded per provider. Market-based reported alongside.**

**Step 5 — construction. Construction \= E\_fac × k\_c, k\_c \= 0.007 kgCO₂e/kWh, applied post-PUE.**

**Step 6 — embodied IT hardware. Expressed per kWh of accelerator energy so it applies directly to CLEER output:**

I\_emb \= M ÷ (L × 8,760 × P̄\_tray × TDP\_tray) Embodied \= (E\_acc \+ E\_dev) × I\_emb

M is 5,325 kgCO₂e GPU-served or 2,748 TPU-served (§8.3). L is 3 years, applied to both classes since its evidentiary basis does not vary by vendor.

\*\*P̄\_tray**, average tray power over life as a share of the 8-accelerator tray’s 5.6 kW TDP.** Default 40%\*\*, set below the midpoint of the empirical range: a production inference deployment using continuous batching is reported moving from 22% to 68% utilization upon optimization. Landing below the midpoint preserves the conservative reading, since a lower assumed draw carries the same embodied mass over fewer lifetime kWh and raises I\_emb.

At the default: **`I_emb ≈ 90 gCO₂e/kWh`** accelerator energy, GPU-served; **`≈ 47`** TPU-served

Sensitivity: 164 g/kWh at 22% TDP, 53 at 68%, 36 at a 100%-utilization structural floor.

*Not used:* survey figures reporting \~5% average enterprise GPU utilization across general Kubernetes clusters. That measures general enterprise deployments, not hyperscaler frontier-model serving fleets under continuous cost pressure; adopting it would understate P̄\_tray for a population-mismatch reason, not a conservatism one. Nor is the default contradicted by production node-power figures centered on 70% of maximum draw: those are instantaneous power while actively serving, whereas P̄\_tray is average tray power across the entire installed life, including provisioned-but-idle periods accounted for separately on the energy side.

**Step 7 — reported total.**

Reported (LB) \= Operational \+ Construction \+ Embodied

The model-development component is disclosed within the reported total as a separate line, together with the data level from which d was taken (§11.4). It is not held outside the inventory.

## Worked example

A period with 80.3 MWh of serving accelerator energy, GPU-served, rung 3 grid factor, d \= 1.5.

| Term | Calculation | tCO₂e |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Development accelerator energy | 80.3 MWh × d 1.5 | 120.5 MWh |
| Facility energy | 80.3 × 2.3925 \+ 120.5 × 2.175 | 454.1 MWh |
| Operational (LB) | 454.1 MWh × 0.341 kg/kWh | 154.9 |
| DC construction | 454.1 MWh × 7 g/kWh | 3.2 |
| Embodied IT | 200.8 MWh × 90 g/kWh | 18.1 |
| **Reported total (LB)** |  | **176.1** |
| of which model development | disclosed within the total | 102.0 |

Model development contributes 102.0 tCO₂e, 58% of the reported total. Construction lands at 2.1% of operational and 1.8% of the total; embodied at 10.3% of the total, in line with Google’s \~10% rule of thumb, the \~8% location-based share Jouppi et al. (2026) report for Ironwood, and Mistral’s 11% cross-check.

## Boundary integrity checks

Five non-overlap conditions hold by construction:

1. CLEER estimates accelerator energy only. The host, idle and PUE uplifts each cover a component CLEER does not estimate, so no term is counted twice.

2. The idle uplift covers provisioned-but-idle machines; CLEER’s batching and utilization modeling covers energy within active serving. The terms are disjoint.

3. Host uplift components (fans, PSU losses, storage) are IT load, inside the numerator of the IT energy PUE scales, so host and PUE do not overlap.

4. NVIDIA’s 0.4% PCF transport line is inbound material transport inside cradle-to-gate; the §8.2 distribution uplift covers the separate gate-to-site leg. Construction applies to facility kWh post-PUE; embodied IT applies to accelerator kWh pre-uplift. Neither is scaled twice.

5. Development energy is disjoint from all serving energy. d is a ratio of a provider’s development compute to its serving compute, and is applied to serving accelerator energy before any uplift, so no facility term is applied twice and no serving energy is counted as development.

**Per-period inputs:** token counts by model via the activity bridge; the CLEER intensity table version; the tool, factor and model-coverage register versions. Nothing else changes between periods unless a §13.4 trigger fires.

# 13. Uncertainty

The inventory reports a **single central estimate**, as the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard requires. Uncertainty is not embedded in the reported figure. Conservatism enters through factor selection, not through reporting upper bounds: inflating the reported value beyond the central estimate violates the accuracy principle as surely as understating it.

Two tracks are distinguished because the two kinds of uncertainty propagate differently.

## 13.1 Track 1 — statistical uncertainty in the CLEER estimates

u(E\_acc(m)) \= Tᵢₙ(m)·σᵢₙ(m) \+ T\_c(m)·r(m)·σᵢₙ(m) \+ Tₒᵤₜ(m)·σₒᵤₜ(m)

**Cached tokens.** The middle term carries r(m) × σᵢₙ(m), not r(m) × the cached mean — see §4.5. Where cached tokens carry a large share of energy, which is typical of agentic and long-context tools, mis-propagating this term materially suppresses the band.

**Why linear in token count.** σ can be read two ways, and they propagate in opposite directions. If σ were query-to-query dispersion, individual queries would be independent draws, uncertainty on their sum would grow only as σ√N, and relative uncertainty would vanish at scale. At production volumes that component is negligible: it averages away. What remains, and what the inventory carries, is **model-level calibration error with the same sign for every token of that model**. It does not average down; it scales linearly with volume, giving relative uncertainty σ/ē constant in T. This is consistent with how σ is constructed — it carries the clustering match, the EP8 extrapolation and percentile variability, all model-level, not query-level.

**Across models.** The correlation structure of CLEER’s errors across models is not established: models share calibration sources, a common donor pool and common assumptions, so independence cannot be assumed. Rather than defend a partial-correlation model, the bounding case is adopted — absolute uncertainties summed linearly, equivalent to perfect correlation:

u(E\_acc) \= Σₘ u(E\_acc(m))

**No confidence percentage is claimed, and this is deliberate.** Coverage of this band depends on the correlation structure. Under perfect correlation it is one standard deviation, \~68% coverage. Under independence the same absolute band is typically 2–2.5 sigmas, \~95–98% coverage. No partial-correlation model is asserted. The band is reported as a **bound with its construction described**, which is a stronger and more defensible claim than a confidence interval that cannot be substantiated. A reported band should be labeled accordingly and not described as a confidence interval.

**Skewed distributions.** Where a line’s underlying inputs are right-skewed rather than symmetric — typical of §7.4 hardware classes with lognormal token or energy terms — a symmetric mean ± σ band misrepresents both ends and can go negative at two standard deviations. Take the band as the 15.87th and 84.13th percentiles instead, which correspond to ±1σ on a symmetric distribution, so the label stays consistent across lines while respecting the shape. Where closed-form percentiles are needed, a moment-matched lognormal (Fenton–Wilkinson) is acceptable if validated against simulation and its direction of error disclosed.

**Aggregation across tools.** Low, central and high are summed directly. Root-sum-square would produce a narrower band; the direct sum is the conservative convention and is applied consistently.

## 13.2 Track 2 — systematic uncertainty

The idle factor, PUE, networking treatment, grid intensity, hardware lifespan, embodied accelerator term, the model-development ratio d, and activity-data selections are not random variables. They are selections among defensible alternatives, and any error is identical across all models and tokens. They are presented as discrete scenarios, not folded into a statistical distribution.

**Activity-data uncertainty belongs here, not in Track 1\.** This is new in v2.0. Where a reporting period is incomplete and volumes are back-cast (§5.2 element 4), or where a bridge parameter is selected from a defensible range, the resulting exposure is a *selection*, not a dispersion. Stacking it into the statistical band would combine two incompatible quantities. Recorded as Track 2 scenario rows instead, typically:

* the back-fill baseline window, where a trend in the driver ratio makes the choice consequential;

* the back-fill ratio treatment, flat versus trend-corrected;

* material bridge parameters where the source evidence supports a range, with the fallback position named.

Each row states the modeled share of the period it affects, so a reviewer can see the exposure without re-deriving it. Where the back-cast covers a large share of the period, this is often the largest Track 2 item and should be presented first.

**Not repeated here:** grid carbon intensity, scenario-tested under the §10.2 ladder; and the host term for TPU-served workloads, which §7.3 resolves by hardware class using first-party data rather than treating as a range.

The model-development ratio carries three Track 2 rows: the spend-to-energy conversion, which is the dominant term and is not quantified by any source relied upon (§11.7); the grid basis applied to development energy (§11.5); and the choice of a single sector value in place of provider-specific values (§11.3). Because d multiplies the serving estimate, an error in per-token intensity propagates into both components; the two terms are correlated and are summed, not combined in quadrature.

## 13.3 Scenarios

Applied to the central value, one alternate per factor in each direction where a defensible alternate exists.

Result \= E\_acc × (host × idle × PUE) × CI

| Scenario | Chain | Δ vs. central |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Central (adopted, GPU-served) | 1.50 × 1.10 × 1.45 | — |
| Host at nameplate ceiling | 1.82 × 1.10 × 1.45 | \+21% |
| Idle at highly utilized fleet | 1.50 × 1.05 × 1.45 | `−4.6%` |
| Idle at low-utilization bound | 1.50 × 1.20 × 1.45 | \+9% |
| PUE at measured hyperscaler fleet | 1.50 × 1.10 × 1.09 | `−25%` |
| PUE at purpose-built AI facility | 1.50 × 1.10 × 1.20 | `−17%` |
| PUE at global data-center average | 1.50 × 1.10 × 1.56 | \+8% |
| DC networking included | × 1.14 on the chain | \+14% |
| Hardware life 6 years | I\_emb halves | `−5% (approx., at a ~10% embodied share)` |
| Compounded upper bound | 1.82 × 1.20 × 1.56 × 1.14 | \+62% |

Plus the Track 2 activity-data rows relevant to the engagement (§13.2).

The compounded upper bound is deliberately implausible: it requires every independent selection to be wrong in the same direction simultaneously. Even that case leaves the §4 exclusion conclusions intact.

## 13.4 Maintenance

Not a per-period exercise. The propagation method and scenario table are fixed at methodology level; each period requires only re-running the arithmetic on that period’s volumes. Reopened only upon:

* the weighted-average relative uncertainty band shifting more than 5% from what is reported here, driven by a change in the composition of high- and low-variance models in the served mix, not by routine model addition or retirement;

* a revision to the CLEER intensity table or its uncertainty ranges;

* a change to any Track 2 factor selection;

* the model-coverage fallback contribution exceeding 1% of reported emissions (§5.4).

A preparer closing a period enters that period’s volumes into fixed propagation arithmetic and a pre-computed scenario table. A reader receives one number, a bounded band around it, and a short menu of one-factor sensitivities.

# 14. Assurance guide

## 14.1 Reviewer’s map

Evidence grades: **A** — first-party measured, or standards-conformant third-party reviewed. **B** — peer-reviewed independent measurement. **C** — modeled, proxy, or selected from a range.

| Input | Value | Grade | Source | Direction if wrong |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Per-token accelerator energy | Per model | B | CLEER benchmarking \+ clustering (§6); validated to \<1% on DeepSeek deployment reconstruction | Two-sided; flagged per model by confidence score |
| Host uplift, GPU | 1.50 | B | Measured CPU+DRAM offset 366.5 W (§7.2) × documented remainder; corroborated by metered H100 node and GB200 reference | Understates if accelerators ran below TDP |
| Host uplift, TPU | 1.43 | A | Google production fleet disclosure | — |
| Idle uplift | 1.10 | B | Google fleet; independently adopted by Oviedo et al. | Two-sided |
| PUE | 1.45 | C | LBNL US average; deliberately not a hyperscaler figure (§10.1) | Overstates if workloads are served from purpose-built campuses |
| Grid CI, rung 3 | 0.341 | A | EPA eGRID code, 2024 inputs, Cornerstone reconstruction | Understates — data centers run \~48% above national average |
| Grid CI, rung 4 | 0.730 | B | O’Donoughue harmonization \+ Alvarez measured leakage | Understates; both available adjustments push upward |
| Model-development ratio d | 1.5 | C | Epoch AI 2026 company spending reconstruction; SemiAnalysis 2026 compute allocation. Two independent methods agreeing to within 2% (§11.3) | Understates; a spending ratio does not capture the higher energy intensity per dollar of development compute |
| Embodied, accelerator | 1,312 kgCO₂e (H100 baseboard) | A | NVIDIA PCF, ISO 14067, WSP-reviewed | May understate by \~43% per ADEME parametric comparison (§8.1) |
| Host tray uplift | × 3.62 | B | Boavizta and EcoServe convergence at 72.4–75% | Two-sided within the 72.4–75% bracket |
| Distribution uplift | × 1.12 | B | Three air-freight models, 1.06–1.21 | Understates if sourced from the top of the range |
| Hardware life | 3 years | C | Conservatism call; practitioner range 3–6 (§8.3) | Overstates; 6 years halves the embodied term |
| P̄\_tray | 40% TDP | C | Below the midpoint of a 22–68% empirical range | Overstates |
| Construction | 7 gCO₂e/kWh | B | Google TPU LCA, five generations; Carbon Trust cross-check at 5.3 | Two-sided; ±30% between the two anchors |
| Cache-read ratio | r(m), per model | C | Provider published pricing; a price standing for an energy ratio (§4.5) | Not established |
| Activity data | Per tool | Varies | Tool telemetry, or bridge (§5.2) | Per bridge document |

## 14.2 What to test

1. **Reconcile activity data to source.** Token counts or the bridge’s input telemetry, to provider-exported reports for the period. This is the one input the customer controls and the only one with a documentary trail.

2. **Confirm register versions.** The tool, factor and CLEER table versions used to produce the figure should match those recorded, and any change should be a version event, not a period adjustment.

3. **Check the model-coverage statement** `(§5.4): coverage ≥ 99.9%, fallback contribution < 1%, branch applied per unmatched model.`

4. **Verify no double-counting** against the four boundary integrity checks in §12.

5. **Test the estimator in each bridge.** The most common defect is a percentile substituted for a mean (§5.2), which overstates by two to six times.

6. **Check the cached-token treatment** on both mean and standard deviation (§4.5), since the SD rule is easy to get wrong and suppresses the reported band when it is.

7. **Confirm the grid rung assignment** per provider against the evidence recorded in the factor register.

Confirm the model-development treatment. d should be applied to serving accelerator energy before any uplift, the development path should omit the idle uplift (§11.5), and the component should appear as a disclosed line within the reported total rather than outside it.

8. **Confirm conservatism is applied once.** It belongs in factor selection, not in the reported figure. A reported figure above the central estimate is itself a finding.

## 14.3 Where the estimate is weakest

Four, stated plainly rather than left to be found.

**Facility attribution.** No provider discloses which site served which request, so the rung structures in §10 are a workaround, not a solution. Both PUE and grid factor inherit that gap. Remedy: serving region and facility PUE per request.

**The embodied accelerator term.** Two studies of the same part differ by \~43% for reasons of background database selection, not inventory, and neither can be shown correct from the published record (§8.1). Remedy: convergence in the embodied carbon literature on background data, which is outside any party’s control here.

**Hardware lifespan.** The practitioner range spans a factor of two on evidence supporting no point within it (§8.3). Remedy: fleet survival data on current-generation hardware.

The model-development ratio. The values available are ratios of compute spending rather than of energy, and no source relied upon quantifies the difference between the two (§11.7). No provider in the register publishes the ratio directly. Remedy: a provider disclosure of development and serving energy, which would move the input from a sector value to a provider-specific one and from a spending basis to an energy basis.

All three are **disclosure problems, not modeling problems**. Each has a specific remedy, and the methodology is built so that each disclosure, if made, replaces an estimate with an observation without altering the structure of the calculation.

# 15. What this methodology does and does not establish

**What it is.** An estimate of greenhouse gas emissions attributable to a customer’s use of third-party generative AI services over a defined period, assembled from token counts the customer can evidence, per-token accelerator intensities measured on open models under production-representative conditions and extrapolated to closed models through architectural clustering, and a documented chain of uplift, conversion and amortization factors each traced to a primary source. It covers operational energy across accelerator, host and facility; embodied carbon of serving hardware and of the buildings housing it; and conversion to carbon on both a location-based and a market-based basis.

**What it is not.** A measurement. No consumer of a closed model can measure the energy drawn by an inference request, and nothing here claims otherwise. Three parameters in particular stand in for quantities only the provider can observe: per-token accelerator intensity, the efficiency of the facility that served the request, and the carbon intensity of the electricity that facility drew.

**Why it is nonetheless defensible.** Three disciplines run through the document. Every numerical claim traces to a primary source, not a secondary summary. Where a parameter cannot be resolved from the evidence it is defaulted in the direction that does not flatter the result, and the choice is labeled a conservatism call rather than presented as an empirical finding. And where the evidence is genuinely contested, the contest is disclosed in the text rather than settled silently in a spreadsheet.

**Maintenance.** The methodology, its companion bridge documents and its registers are versioned together. A change to any factor is a version event, not a period adjustment, and the conditions that reopen a factor are set out in §13.4.
